national.title: NPR's Student Podcast Challenge is back for 2027
national.summary: The annual audio competition for grades four through 12 returns in January. Now in its ninth year, the contest has involved more than 90,000 students around the country.
national.body:
Enlarge this image LA Johnson /NPR LA Johnson /NPR Students and teachers, it's time to turn on your microphones and start recording – in January, the NPR Student Podcast Challenge returns for its ninth year.

Since its launch in 2018, our annual audio storytelling competition for students in grades four through 12 has introduced more than 90,000 students to the world of podcasting.

During that time we've heard from students, teachers, parents and educators around the country about how they've enjoyed participating – and how much they've learned along the way.

"I can't tell you how many of my students come back to tell me this project was the most meaningful thing they did while in middle school," says Laura Frisbie, an advanced learning teacher at Minnetonka Middle School West, in Excelsior, Minn. "What a powerful way for students to use their voices in an authentic way and share a message that is important to them."

Student Podcast Challenge For teachers coming to the competition for the first time, maybe looking to shake things up in your classroom and try something new, we've got tons of resources available to help you get started. And for our returning educators, there's plenty there to draw on to help your students get better.

The 2027 competition will open Jan. 4, to students in grades four through 12. You'll have until May 30 to submit. Grand prize winners will be announced after summer break in September.

Our NPR education team will listen to every single one (more than 22,000 podcasts so far!) and narrow them down to a list of finalists and honorable mentions.

From those entries, our judges will select the grand-prize winners: one for grades five through eight, and another in grades nine through 12. Since 2024, we've also opened our contest to fourth-graders , and we choose winners and honorable mentions from that category as well.

national.title: As millions lose food aid nationwide, this SNAP office is doubling up as a food pantry
national.summary: The cuts and changes to SNAP have been difficult for government workers who take pride in helping others. In San Diego, workers said they couldn't sit back while their neighbors went hungry.
national.body:
Rosa Rodarte, a human services specialist for San Diego County, helps an attendee load groceries into their truck at a food distribution event in the Kearny Mesa neighborhood. Kori Suzuki for NPR hide caption

SAN DIEGO, CALIF. — It should have been her day off. Instead, early Saturday morning, Rosa Rodarte was back at the social service office where she works, pushing carts of food and loading them into people's cars.

Rodarte's official job is to help people apply for programs like food assistance. But lately, she's been simply helping people get food.

"We have the same goal," she says. "We want to make sure everybody is being helped and not judged."

Sacks of red onions and oranges ready to be distributed at food distribution event in San Diego. Kori Suzuki for NPR hide caption

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as SNAP, has seen participation plummet over the past year. Some five million people nationwide have lost federal food benefits ever since the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill, a piece of sweeping tax and spending legislation that slashed SNAP funding, tightened eligibility, and prohibited food aid for most asylum seekers and refugees. It's considered the fastest decline in decades and far exceeding the federal government's own estimates of the impacts.

National SNAP's funding model is starting to change. Here's what that means for the program Not only has it been difficult for families facing food insecurity, but it's also taken a toll on the government workers who help administer SNAP. Over the past year, offices across the country have had to contend with new rules, heavier workloads and immense financial pressure to avoid errors. All the while, they've watched people lose food assistance en masse.

"The emotionally draining part is where you see someone that's telling you on the phone that they need your help and they need it today, and when you can't do something," says Nina Olivas, who oversees San Diego's Access Customer Service Call Center, where people inquire about assistance programs, such as SNAP or Medicaid.

national.title: Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
national.summary: The trip to China marks Trump's second time this year, and comes as the president and his party faced widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections.
national.body:
President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit.

The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year, and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections, potentially weakening his bargaining position across the Pacific.

The president and administration officials – including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – are also under scrutiny after the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , who admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

Huang traveled to China with Trump earlier this year – this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen.

The expectation for major deals or pronouncements coming out of the meetings this week are low – but the meeting is still expected to make waves over the imagery of the trilateral summit.

Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines where he'll meet with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila.

The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days.

For weeks the president has said he's keen to discuss the Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. But Edgard Kagan, the former ambassador to Malaysia and a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said it's a topic that Xi likely won't want to get into. The White House confirmed Friday that Trump is expected to meet with Xi and Putin together.

national.title: These birds fly 17,000 miles every year. Climate change could make it harder
national.summary: Migratory birds cross the entire globe, carefully timing their journeys with the seasons. In a hotter climate, that timing is increasingly out of sync.
national.body:
Pectoral sandpipers are among more than 12 million shorebirds that migrate to Alaska every year to breed. For years, scientists have been trying to understand how these unassuming birds make such monumental journeys. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Pectoral sandpipers are ultra-marathoners. They fly more than 17,000 miles a year, crossing entire continents on their migration from Alaska to Argentina and back again. They don't soar or coast on the wind – they flap the entire way. And these elite athletes are only the size of a robin, weighing around three ounces.

The sandpipers are among more than 12 million shorebirds that migrate to Alaska every year to breed, spending the short summer season in open lands near water. For years, scientists have been trying to understand how these unassuming birds accomplish such monumental journeys from places like New Zealand, Asia, South America.

Rick Lanctot studies shorebirds with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. He marvels at the adaptations that allow the birds to make such long migrations. "All of the organs that they don't need during a nonstop migration get really tiny, like their digestive system shrinks," Lanctot says. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

"Shorebirds are not these little brown birds on the beach, but they're miraculous migrants that travel these huge distances by these crazy adaptations," says Rick Lanctot, a wildlife biologist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

For 24 years, Lanctot and other researchers have tracked the return of shorebirds to northern Alaska. The data shows a concerning trend. Overall, almost half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are declining . Some have lost more than half of their population over the last 30 years.

Ryan Kellman/NPR Clockwise from top: A pectoral sandpiper, two red-necked phalarope, and a dunlin being tagged by a researcher are all examples of the 41 species of shorebirds that breed in Alaska. Nearly half of those species are declining. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Migration, like any kind of travel, requires careful timing. Birds orchestrate their journeys to take advantage of the seasons, arriving when food is ample and the weather is ideal. But for many species, their itineraries are going increasingly awry. Habitats they count on, such as wetlands and grasslands, are disappearing. In a hotter climate, spring is arriving earlier, which affects when their food is available. It's like making a pit stop on a road trip and finding all the restaurants are closed.

national.title: 'You're going to win the war': Harry praises war veterans on surprise Ukraine visit
national.summary: He has been showing support for injured veterans in Ukraine and praising the country's resilience.
national.body:
Royal correspondent , Reporting from Lviv, Ukraine Published 15 November 2026 Updated 55 minutes ago The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.

There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."

Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.

Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.

"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.

A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.

At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.

International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.

national.title: Airline schedules returning to normal after ground stop, FAA says
national.summary: Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.
national.body: Operations were returning to normal or close to it at most major airlines early Monday after a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, causing chaos in the nation's airports with thousands of flights canceled and travelers stranded.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that travelers should expect delays to continue but "we should be running at full capacity" heading into Monday."What happens with a ground stop, like on Friday, we have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations, but we're well on our way," he said.Still, more than 2,300 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were canceled Sunday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware and more than 10,400 were delayed, though not necessarily as a result of ripple effects from the ground stop.FlightAware said more than 250 Monday flights had been canceled and 650 delayed as of 4:00 a.m. EST.How did the FAA ground stop happen?The ground stop began at 3:36 p.m. ET Friday when the FAA ordered the stoppage while approximately 3,500 flights were in the air."The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air," Duffy said. All airborne planes were able to land safely.It was lifted around 8:20 p.m. ET Friday.This marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last national ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware, stranding passengers at major airports across the country. Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology."It's just the FAA is still using this really old telecom network that has to be updated, upgraded, and I think built brand new," Duffy said on "Face the Nation" on Sunday.Duffy told reporters on Saturday that a preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working in a remote FAA location and switching old copper wire to fiber while replacing a router. national.summary: The attacks come after the U.S. carried out minor strikes on Iran's Qeshm island in recent weeks.

Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Monday, November 16, here. See earlier developments below.

A U.S. military official confirmed to CBS News that the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt is now in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, which were already operating in the region. The three-carrier presence is expected to be temporary as carrier strike groups rotate through the region.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, on Sunday rejected Germany's demand that Tehran halt uranium enrichment, saying the country has a right to enrich uranium as a member of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty.

Baghaei also criticized the U.N. nuclear watchdog — the International Atomic Energy Agency — for what he described as "nontechnical speculation" about a possible new uranium enrichment facility in the central Iranian city of Isfahan. He claimed Iran had not suspended its safeguards obligations.

A U.S. Army soldier who survived a deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran .

The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes ' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Friday and obtained by CBS News.

He alleges Army leaders dismissed concerns over thin fortifications at a U.S. command post in Kuwait where six American soldiers were killed by an Iranian drone in the first 24 hours of the conflict, the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the war.

The complaint also claims the post — known as Port Shuaiba — "had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance."

national.title: UK and allies call on Israel to allow rapid humanitarian access to Gaza
national.summary: The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy say Israeli authorities are holding back vital supplies at the borders, including 150,00 tents.
national.body:
The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy have issued a joint statement urging Israel to "allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza", where they say the situation on the ground is "dire".

The foreign ministers warn recent floods have brought "further suffering" to the war-torn territory, which recently had its first winter storm.

The statement says 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border.

The Israeli military authority which controls the Gaza crossings has said it is co-ordinating with the US-led Board of Peace and the UN on a winter plan, and that 93,000 tents and 8,600 aid trucks with winter supplies had entered the territory.

It added that reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".

The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said the widespread flooding and a landslide led to a number of deaths, thousands of damaged shelters and the suspension of critical services.

The statement from the British, Australian, Canadian and Italian foreign ministers says , external : "This situation is entirely reversible - and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in."

"The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late."

national.body: A British naval monitoring agency said Monday morning it had received a report of a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz being struck. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center said the vessel was "struck by an unknown projectile whilst transiting outbound," resulting in a fire in the engine room. It added that crew members were all accounted for and no casualties were reported. Meanwhile, Iran's state broadcaster said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz had caught fire after hitting a naval mine, citing Tehran's navy. It said the ship was traveling through a "restricted area," which "exposes offending vessels to serious risks." Iran's armed forces regularly report similar incidents with ships Tehran deems to be transiting the Strait of Hormuz without its permission.

national.title: 4 NFL officials work 2 games each due to ground stop, a rarity
national.summary: Four NFL officials worked two games Sunday — a rarity stemming from Friday's nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA that threw airlines' schedules into complete disarray.
national.body: Cincinnati — Don Willard did something on Sunday that the NFL hopes doesn't ever have to be duplicated — refereeing two games in one day.Willard was the referee Sunday afternoon for the Miami Dolphins' game against the Indianapolis Colts in Indianapolis before he and three other members of the crew made the 114-mile trip to work the prime-time contest between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals.The reshuffling happened after the Federal Aviation Administration called for a nationwide ground stop Friday. The stop caused consternation and chaos for professional and college teams throughout the country and even resulted in moving at least one college football game from Saturday to Sunday. NFL officials audibled by reassigning game officials for this week's matchups to stadiums closer to cities where they reside so they could drive, and Willard was asked to take over as the lead ref for the two games. Willard usually works NFL games as a side judge. About an hour before kickoff in Indianapolis, he did the traditional microphone check and then he handled the coin toss duties typically reserved for referees. Willard wasn't the only one doing double duty Sunday. Umpire Terry Killens, field judge Jabir Walker and side judge Justin Larrew also jumped in a minibus and made the two-hour drive down I-74 to work the game in Cincinnati. It's the first time this officiating crew has worked together. The four officials arrived in Cincinnati at 6:39 p.m., giving them some time to prepare before the 8:20 p.m. kickoff. There were two instant replay reversals during the first half. A 23-yard completion to Pittsburgh's Germie Bernard was overturned when replay saw Bernard's toe was just out of bounds. An interception by Cincinnati's Jordan Battle was also reversed when a second look showed the ball hit the ground. However, the crew called only 12 penalties in a game that usually sees a lot of flags because of the intensity of the Steelers-Bengals rivalry. "I thought they did a great job managing a very difficult game, very testy game, obviously by both sides. So hats off to those guys for what they pulled off today. I know it was a long day for them," Bengals coach Zac Taylor said. League officials didn't make any of the four officials who did double duty available to the media for either of Sunday's games. national.title: US basketball player arrested with 34kg of cannabis at Nigerian airport
national.summary: The anti-drugs agency says the American attempted to leave the airport, abandoning his luggage with the drugs.
national.body:
A basketball player from the US has been arrested in Nigeria with 33.95kg (75lbs) of cannabis in his luggage at the main airport in Lagos.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) identified the player as Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, from the US state of Georgia, who it said had arrived from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

According to the agency, the suspect said he had been playing professional basketball in Thailand and was visiting to Nigeria to "build networks" for his career. He has not publicly commented on the allegations.

The agency said an examination of the suspect's phone had pointed "to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity".

In statement on Sunday, the agency said he was arrested on Wednesday after airport officials noticed him abandoning his two checked-in bags and attempting to leave with his carry-on bag.

The two bags, which bore his name, contained 32 packs of the drug known as "Loud", a potent strain of cannabis, the agency said.

A tracking device was also recovered from the bags, the agency added.

The International Basketball Federation (FIBA) lists a player by the name Damonte Greene, with the most recent appearance at the Phuket Elite Cup in Thailand, on 26 September.

national.title: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key area on coast of Red Sea waterway
national.summary: Saudi-backed forces say they are moving troops from the Bab al-Mandab Strait to defend the interim capital Aden.
national.body:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.

Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.

The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.

Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.

But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".

The Southern Armed Forces' statement said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".

It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".

national.title: Wife of assassinated ex-Haitian leader registers for presidential election
national.summary: There has not been an election in Haiti since before the death of Jovenel Moise in 2021.
national.body:
The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation.

Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021.

Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence.

Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity.

Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday.

Last week she said on X: "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently."

A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy.

Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021 , allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries.

national.title: Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
national.summary: Rescuers found the pet cat in the ruins of Zariah's apartment four days after she made an emotional plea to the public.
national.body:
Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse Close A teenage girl and her cat have been reunited four days after a building in the New York borough of Brooklyn collapsed.

Zariah Coleman, 13, made an emotional plea when her pet went missing after she and her family were forced to relocate when the side of their building was stripped off in the unexpected collapse.

City officials later found her cat, Isaac, in the debris of the their home and shared the reunion on Sunday afternoon.

Eight people died and 18 others were injured when the three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood last Wednesday.

national.title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo dies age 80
national.summary: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.
national.body:
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.

Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.

Known as The Godfather or the "Boss of Bosses", Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.

At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.

The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.

He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.

At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.

At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.

national.title: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack

national.body:
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.

The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.

In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.

"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.

"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."

She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.

Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.

national.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
national.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
national.body:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director of Megaspeed near the end of 2023, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS but it said she was still "practically in control" of the company.

Alice Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.

national.title: Flight disruptions expected to last into Monday
national.summary: Congress recently gave the Department of Transportation $12.5 billion to upgrade the aging air traffic control system. President Trump wants more.
national.body:
Aircraft are seen at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption

Thousands of travelers are still waiting on airlines to reschedule cancelled flights after Friday's nationwide ground stop.

More than 2,300 flights have been cancelled and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. are delayed as of Sunday evening, according to FlightAware.com . Airports in Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta were experiencing the largest number of delays, with more than 250 flights each.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that "by the end of today, end of tomorrow, I think we will be back to normal."

"What happens when you have a ground stop like what happened on Friday is we have airplanes and air crews that are out of position," Duffy said during an interview with NBC's Meet The Press . "It takes some time for the airlines to re-choreograph all of their crews and aircraft."

Duffy on Saturday blamed faulty maintenance by L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, for the nationwide ground stop.

L3Harris was working on replacing two sections of old copper wire with new fiber-optic cables, Duffy said. At some point, the FAA's legacy equipment became overloaded and disrupted communications.

"The initial investigation indicates that two potential locations as the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas."

national.title: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
national.summary: Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month.
national.body:
Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.

Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.

The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.

Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.

On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.

A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.

He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".

national.summary: In his first TV interview, Billy Evans, partner of disgraced Theranos co-founder Elizabeth Holmes, talks about his characterization in the documentary "You Can See Everything," as well as threats he says have been made against his family's safety.
national.body: Billy Evans may be the most-talked-about person in the most-talked-about film of the year, the documentary "You Can See Everything." He sat down with "CBS Sunday Morning" for his first-ever TV interview. Why now? "You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life," he said. "And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is, 'You can't lose your voice.'""You Can See Everything" is a film by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, who shot to fame as an absurdist comedian, and who (along with cameras) moved in with Evans and his partner Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison in 2023.Evans, a 34-year-old MIT grad who'd also worked in high-tech, emerges as a shape-shifting central character. Asked if he is the person we saw in the film, or something else, Evans said, "I'm deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do. But no, I am not some controlling monster who's leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things."It's easy to understand why the genre-bending film has become a cultural phenomenon … harder to understand why Evans agreed to do it. "I think sometimes I take too big of risks," he said. Such as? "Inviting Nathan Fielder into your home for 34 days and trusting somebody to have the right to portray you in any way, shape or form that they so choose."In the film, Evans is portrayed as a villain – controlling and manipulative. Yet, Evans doesn't seem angry about that: "It's super-painful, but me being angry about it doesn't help change it. Look, I'm going to live my life with integrity and with who I am, and I hope people can see that over time. national.title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
national.summary: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power
national.body:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.

More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.

Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.

"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."

In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.

That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.

And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.

But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.

national.title: Libyan town rebuilt after devastating floods becomes showcase for strongman's rule
national.summary: The remarkable reconstruction of Derna is being used as a showcase for the rest of Libya by Khalifa Haftar and his sons.
national.body:
"It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna.

Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him.

Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya.

It is part of a rapid $2bn (£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.

The money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption.

Damdoum, like many flood survivors, simply thanks the head of the Development and Reconstruction Fund, Belkacem Haftar, for what has been achieved since the early hours of 11 September 2023, when lashing rain from Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, sending a wall of water 7m (23 ft) high cascading down onto the sleeping city.

The exact death toll will probably never be known. Some estimates have been as high as 6,000, though 4,000 now seems a more likely figure. Many bodies are still unidentified.

In a city of about 100,000 people, that means almost everybody lost someone they loved. The 14 relatives and neighbours on the roof with Damdoum – including his father, brother and sister - all drowned.

national.title: Thousands of US flights still cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
national.summary: The US transport secretary says that normal air-traffic operations may not be restored until Monday.
national.body:
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.

"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 8,800 flights were delayed and 2,400 cancelled on Sunday.

President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.

The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.

The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.

The sales of kratom in the U.S. have fueled a billion-dollar industry, with products containing the plant available online and in tens of thousands of stores across the country, including gas stations. The kratom industry hails the substance as a mild stimulant that can also aid in recovery from opioid addiction. The kratom industry has supporters in the highest ranks of government and is legally sold in most states. But health experts warn that kratom use can lead to addiction and death. national.summary: Here are some of the takeaways from our interview with actor John Malkovich following the release of his latest movie, "Wild Horse Nine."
national.body: With his latest movie, "Wild Horse Nine," out in theaters, actor John Malkovich sat down with 60 Minutes and reflected on his decades-long career.Here are four takeaways from the interview:Over his long career, Malkovich says he's only read 6 scripts he considers truly greatThe actor said 1988's "Dangerous Liaisons" is one of just a handful of truly great scripts he's read in his 50-year career. "Great characters, and a fantastic adaptation by Christopher Hampton, whose writing I did and still respect a great deal," Malkovich said.He chalks up other movies to interesting ideas with great parts, including his "In the Line of Fire" role, which earned Malkovich his second Oscar nomination. Malkovich says there's "been a loss of making characters that an audience simply cares about"In "Wild Horse Nine," a black comedy set on Chile's Easter Island months before the engineered coup d'etat in 1973, Malkovich plays Chris, a spy reckoning with the ghosts of assassinations and unsavory actions. "I think there has been a loss of making characters that an audience simply cares about, whether they're salvageable or redeemable people who've done terrible things, or just terrible people," Malkovich said. The movie deals with a dark subject matter, but features hilarious dialogue. "When you have great writing, you can go from something remarkably sad in a millisecond to something very funny and all that's forgotten, all that's forgiven," Malkovich said. The actor thought "Being John Malkovich" should be "Being Tom Cruise"Malkovich tried to convince screenwriter Charlie Kaufman to use a different actor in 1998's "Being John Malkovich." national.title: Officials say a tanker's steering failed before it crashed into a cruise ship in New Orleans
national.summary: The preliminary finding from National Transportation Safety Board officials provided the first official word on what caused Friday's crash of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker into the American Heritage cruise ship, which sent passengers, crew and two police officers plunging into the Mississippi River.
national.body:
A tanker's steering system failed and kept its rudder in a position that sent it crashing into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans, U.S. government safety officials said Sunday.

The preliminary finding from National Transportation Safety Board officials provided the first official word on what caused Friday's crash of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker into the American Heritage cruise ship, which sent passengers, crew and two police officers plunging into the Mississippi River.

NTSB officials said during a briefing in New Orleans that it's not yet clear what caused the steering failure.

"It could be many different things," NTSB accident investigator Bart Barnum said. "That is something that we're investigating very closely."

The tanker, measuring about 520 feet (160 meters) long, had a crew of 19. The cruise ship, about 300 feet (91 meters) long, had 140 passengers and 50 crew onboard.

Officials said 32 people were taken to the hospital, including the two police officers who were thrown into the river when the boat rolled, but none of the injuries were critical. As of Sunday, six people remained hospitalized, the city of New Orleans said in a statement.

The tanker's steering problem caused its rudder to remain in a starboard position, to the right, which sent the tanker veering toward the east bank of the river, where it hit the cruise ship two minutes after the rudder became stuck, Barnum said.

As the tanker approached the river's east bank, the ship's data recorder captured audio sounds "consistent" with the ship's whistle going off, along with warnings and requests for assistance broadcast over the vessel's marine radio, Barnum said. He added the data included commands to deploy the vessel anchors and emergency ship handling orders.

It remains unclear what caused the "steering casualty" on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a media briefing on Sunday.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken American Heritage riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for.

The NTSB said there are many different things that could be classified as a steering casualty, and they are "looking at all of them".

national.title: Trump's handpicked party chair faces a rebellion as midterm losses challenge president's grip on GOP
national.summary: The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump's dominance, even after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation.
national.body:
Steve Peoples, Associated Press Steve Peoples, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump's handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it's already getting ugly.

Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump's former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don't fall in line.

The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump's dominance, even after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the heavy losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies.

But inside the RNC, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party's national political operation, a small yet growing group is backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge.

The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky's KC Crosbie, the RNC's second-in-command, who launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters' allies.

Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his "Make America Great Again" agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power.

"We have an obligation to serve the Republican Party the most effective way we can. And if all we do is say yes to what the White House wants, I'm not sure that's doing what's best for the Republican Party," said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie's candidacy. "Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time."

national.title: Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space
national.summary: NASA's Voyager 1, which is the furthest man-made object from Earth, is set to reach a new milestone this week. On Wednesday, the probe will be roughly 16 billion miles from Earth.
national.body:
This illustration provided by NASA depicts Voyager 1. AP/NASA hide caption

NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than anything else that humans have launched into space. On Wednesday, it's set to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that is one-light day away from Earth.

NASA is celebrating the occasion with the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day . " Calling it a symbolic celebration, NASA is asking the public on Tuesday night to send Voyager's call sign V-G-R into the sky in morse code. Use a flashlight, phone light or anything that can blink a sequence.

V - Three quick flashes, one long flash G - Two long flashes, one quick flash R - One quick flash, one long flash, one quick flash

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, or more than 16 billion miles.

This NASA spacecraft has traveled for nearly 50 years, launching Sept. 5, 1977.

Over the course of its mission, Voyager 1 has conducted flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1979, it discovered a faint ring system on Jupiter. In 1980, the spacecraft took detailed photos of Saturn's rings and moons.

While on its journey, on Feb. 17, 1998, Voyager 1 overtook the U.S. space probe, Pioneer 10, becoming the most distant human-made object in existence. It and its twin, Voyager 2, are the only spacecraft to have operated outside of the heliosphere, which acts like a protective shield of the solar system.

national.title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
national.summary: The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines.
national.body:
MIAMI (AP) — Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries.

The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said.

On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft.

The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days.

The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said.

In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries.

UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened.

"We cannot speculate on the details of the incident," UPS said in a statement. "The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information."

local.title: NY awards $60M to boost power at former Kodak Park
local.summary: RED Rochester operates the park's utilities. The total project cost is estimated at more than $93 million.
local.body:
Gov. Kathy Hochul says the state will contribute $60 million toward the modernization of Eastman Business Park's power grid.

"The project increases the ability to move electricity across the 1,200-acre campus and into priority development areas," an announcement from governor's office stated.

RED Rochester operates the park's utilities. The total project cost is estimated at more than $93 million, and includes expanding transmission and distribution capability, on-site generation and system stability, resiliency and flexibility, according to the state.

"The improved power capacity at shovel-ready parcels and vacant buildings around the campus enable (sic) attraction of new manufacturers," according to the news release.

Funding comes from the state's POWER-UP or Promote Opportunity with Electric Readiness for Underdeveloped Properties program, helping fund critical electrical infrastructure at key industrial sites in the Finger Lakes and Western New York. The program launched in 2025. Funding for Eastman Business Park was part of the second round of grant awards.

local.title: What happened to the hundreds of asylum seekers NY sent to Rochester?
local.summary: Through the state's Migrant Relocation Assistance Program 178 families eventually relocated to Monroe Country, receiving help with housing and other services as they worked to become self-sufficient, although some left.
local.body:
A state-run program created to relocate asylum seekers out of crowded New York City shelters in 2023 ended up assisting 671 families numbering more than 2,000 adults and children.

Roughly half of those went to two places: Albany and Rochester. The majority came to Rochester, their journey beginning with a bus ride that brought them to a downtown hotel .

Three years later, both the program and the hotel have been shut down. And officials estimate that more than a quarter of the people who came to Rochester have left, returning to New York City, moving elsewhere or leaving the country.

The families were mainly from Central and South America, with some individuals from Haiti and parts of Africa.

They left for a variety of reasons, including limited job opportunities, or fear of being more vulnerable to immigration enforcement in a mid-sized city versus New York City. And there were delays in receiving work authorization, meaning they couldn’t afford to stay, said Daisy Ruiz-Marin, community response lead at Rochester's Ibero-American Action League, which oversaw the state’s Migrant Relocation Assistance Program locally.

"Some folks decided to return back to a New York City shelter,” she said, “because even though Monroe County is more affordable at the time of their graduation (from the state program), there was no way for them to continue being self-sufficient for their family, so they ended up deciding to relocate."

But many have stayed, including a family of three from Nicaragua.

The mother and father found work in retail, while the child enrolled in school — making a home in a city that the mother said she remembers feeling was small and developing when they first arrived.

local.title: Family at home can be big help for deer hunters
local.summary: Families across Western New York are getting ready for two familiar signs of the season: winter weather and the opening of New York’s Southern Zone big game hunting season this coming Saturday. While some families have watched their children grow up and leave the nest, others are just introducing th
local.body:
Families across Western New York are getting ready for two familiar signs of the season: winter weather and the opening of New York’s Southern Zone big game hunting season this coming Saturday.

While some families have watched their children grow up and leave the nest, others are just introducing their youngsters to the traditions of deer hunting. In many households, both mom and dad hunt. In others, mom is the one taking the kids into the woods. Either way, hunting season has a way of bringing families together in any number of ways.

Family members who are not heading out with a hunting license and blaze orange can help make Opening Day special too. The home-stay family may be among the most important members of the Opening Day support crew.

They know that the night before Opening Day is no time to discover that someone’s gloves have disappeared, the flashlight needs batteries or the hunting boots are still sitting in the garage with a sack of spider webs that made a winter home. Hunters almost always need help to check clothing, licenses, required safety equipment, snack supplies, water and other essentials. A thermos of hot coffee or cocoa can earn the home-family honorary family MVP status.

Hunters heading out before daylight, 3:30 a.m. come early, and hunters appreciate a good breakfast. Something warm, filling and easy to eat is a welcome start. Just remember, they don't need a three-course meal when they’re trying to get into the woods before sunrise, just wholesome protein.

Check the forecast, remind their hunters to dress in layers (or not), and make sure they’re prepared for changing conditions. November in Western New York can deliver sunshine, freezing temperatures, rain, snow and wind, sometimes before lunchtime!

Remind everyone to wear the required fluorescent orange or pink clothing, handle firearms responsibly, identify their target and what lies beyond it, and follow all hunting regulations. Firearms should always be unloaded when being transported, and every hunter should know where their companions are once they head for the forest. A responsible hunter never takes a shot unless absolutely certain it is safe. Look beyond the target.

Know where everyone plans to hunt, when they expect to return, and how they can be reached. If plans change, make sure someone at home knows. Never let a hunter feel pressured to take an unsafe shot or stay in dangerous weather just to keep up with expectations.

QUEENSBURY -- One year can make quite a difference and for Clymer/Sherman/Panama's Savannah Whitney it meant being a whole minute faster and jumping from 39th to 14th overall in the New York State Public High School Athletic Association Class C cross country championships at Queensbury High School on Saturday afternoon. The Wolfpack eighth-grader posted a time of 19:03.4 to claim 14th overall in the Class C race, while the winning time was posted by Bronxville sophomore Mia Horgan at 17:40.9 to retain her championship.

Horgan's time was not enough to help Bronxville repeat with the team title as Section VIII's Cold Spring Harbor posted the low score of 58.

In the Class D race, the Frewsburg girls finished sixth with a team score of 173, while Section III's South Lewis claimed the team title at 48.

The Bears were led by senior Grace Gilevski taking 21st in team points and 46th overall at 20:46.8, junior Raegan Cheney came 25th in team and 51st overall at 21:02.2, freshman Skye Carter posted 34 team points and 69th overall at 21:37.3, seventh-grader Alina Whippo ran to 46th team points and 90th overall at 22:54.1, eighth-grader Greta Gilevski was 47th in team and 91st overall at 22:56.9, senior Olivia Nelson ran to 93rd overall at 23:08.2 and sophomore Alexis Darling took 95th at 23:18.8.

Qualifying as an individual, Maple Grove junior Lily Elliss posted the best local time in the Class D race, running a sub-20 time of 19:55.0 to take 28th overall.

Tri-Valley senior Anna Furman finished her high school career with a third-straight state title posting a winning time of 17:57.7, nearly 30 seconds faster than second-place Evelyn Rizzo of Pierson at 18:25.4.

Silver Creek/Dunkirk/Forestville junior Leah Mays and freshman Emma Golembieski both ran in the Class B race and finished within seconds of each other. Mays posted a time of 20:51.3 for 79th place and Golembieski came in 82nd at 20:55.7.

Eastport/South Manor senior Maddie Laezza won the race and posted the second-best overall time for girls at states with 17:27.3, while Section XI's Sayville won the team title with 51 points.

local.body:
OBSERVER Photos by Braden Carmen Dunkirk’s K’vion Tell and Forestville’s Manny Sanchez celebrate during boys varsity basketball games last season.

The Dunkirk and Forestville boys basketball teams will play in an NBA arena Dec. 13.

The schools' varsity and JV teams will compete in the Cleveland Cavaliers' home arena, Dunkirk Athletic Director Kyle Jarrell said at the city Board of Education's November meeting. It's part of a series the Cavs run for high school basketball teams.

The Dunkirk and Forestville junior varsity teams will play at 11 a.m. on Sunday, Dec. 13. The schools' varsity teams are set to tip off at 1 p.m. that day.

And no, it won't conflict with a Buffalo Bills game. The Bills play on Sunday Night football against the Green Bay Packers on Dec. 13, set for an 8:20 p.m. kickoff.

Jarrell said the first thing he told the Cavs' representative when contacted was that they had to make sure it did not conflict with a Bills game. He is promising families that they will be back from Cleveland in time for the game.

A possible complication to that: The Cleveland Browns host the Atlanta Falcons at 1 p.m. Dec. 13. The Browns' home stadium is in downtown Cleveland about a dozen blocks from the Cavs' Rocket Arena, and thousands of extra vehicles will be on roads in the area before the game and after it ends around 4 p.m.

The Dunkirk and Forestville teams will get another unforgettable treat on Saturday night, Dec. 12. They will attend a Cavaliers game against the Golden State Warriors.

local.summary: DRYDEN — After getting out of the Section VI tournament as the Class C champion it was smooth sailing for Wilson and the Lakewomen outscored opponents 12-1 in the New York State Public High School Athletic Association championships to claim the program’s first state title at a perfect 21-0-0 on Sund
local.body:
DRYDEN -- After getting out of the Section VI tournament as the Class C champion it was smooth sailing for Wilson and the Lakewomen outscored opponents 12-1 in the New York State Public High School Athletic Association championships to claim the program's first state title at a perfect 21-0-0 on Sunday at Dryden High School.

Wilson was up against Section V's Kendall in the Far West Regionals a week ago and it took just over a minute for the Lakewomen to get all they needed to advance. Zoey Beck scored from Lilly Gurski in the second minute and Lucy Madan added an insurance goal from Gurski again in the 60th minute while Brooke Urban needed just three saves for the 2-0 clean sheet.

Things only got easier in the state semifinals as Wilson cruised past Section X's St. Lawrence 7-1 at Moravia High School on Saturday. Junior forward Addison Elia put on a show as she scored four goals in the contest, eighth-grader Macaela Boyer provided two goals and an assist, Abigail Labarre scored once and Gurski, Kyra Fellows and Kairi Beck had two assists each.

Wilson remained tied at halftime with Section II's Stillwater, but Gurski struck first and the Lakewomen added two more to secure the first girls soccer state title in Section VI since Allegany-Limestone won in 2017.

MIDDLETOWN -- Section VI also brought home a title for the boys as Lewiston-Porter dominated the Class A competition, outscoring opponents 16-1 in four NYSPHSAA games to secure the first title in program history.

The Lancers made it the second year in a row for Section VI taking home the Class A title, following up East Aurora last season.

Lewiston-Porter first won its subregional against Section V's Pittsford Sutherland 2-0 courtesy of goals by Luke and Wyatt Leardini, then in a subregional match against Section IV's Maine-Endwell the Lancers received four goals from Luke Leardini in a dominant 7-1 win.

The Lancers did not slow down once they got to Middletown High School on Friday, first defeating Section II's Averill Park 4-0 and then on Saturday night they shut out Section III's Jamesville-DeWitt 3-0.

local.summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. (AP) — Geno Smith left the game, came back and then left again — this time, for good. Now, Aaron Glenn and the struggling New York Jets have a serious quarterback question as they take a five-game skid to Los Angeles to face the winless Chargers next week. An ankle injury knock
local.body:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. (AP) -- Geno Smith left the game, came back and then left again -- this time, for good.

Now, Aaron Glenn and the struggling New York Jets have a serious quarterback question as they take a five-game skid to Los Angeles to face the winless Chargers next week.

An ankle injury knocked Smith out of the Jets’ 32-12 loss to the Buffalo Bills in the third quarter Sunday after he missed a series to start the second half to be evaluated for a head injury. Rookie Cade Klubnik stepped in for Smith both times, and could be pressed into making his first NFL start if the veteran can’t go next Sunday.

The Jets also have Will Levis, a second-round pick of Tennessee in 2023, on the practice squad.

Glenn was uncertain if Smith and rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr., who left after the Jets’ first offensive play, had high ankle sprains.

“I don’t know,” Glenn said. “I just know they’re both ankles right now. I’ll end up getting that information sometime next week.”

Smith was 13 of 21 for 148 yards. Klubnik was 11 of 20 for 137 yards with an interception, and ran three times for 26 yards. He was also sacked three times.

“Man, this was as tough as it gets for any young quarterback to go against this front that really does a good job of rushing the passer,” Glenn said. “But just from the naked eye, I thought he did a pretty good job.”

The Board intends to fill the vacancy by appointment. The select
local.body:
SOUTH DAYTON -- The Pine Valley Central School District Board of Education invites qualified district residents interested in serving local students, schools, and the community to apply for a Board seat vacancy created by a resignation.

The Board intends to fill the vacancy by appointment. The selected appointee will serve from January until the next regular school district election on May 18, 2027.

Board of Education members serve without compensation and help guide the district's educational priorities, policies, and responsible use of resources. Appointees must be prepared to attend Board meetings, review meeting materials, participate in required training, maintain legally required confidentiality, and work collaboratively in the interests of all district students. A commitment to public education, thoughtful decision-making, and responsible financial oversight is encouraged.

To be eligible for appointment – which will be verified prior to selection – applicants must meet the following criteria:

-- Have been a continuous district resident for at least one year before taking office.

-- Not be employed by the Board of Education on which they would serve.

-- Not reside in the same household with a family member serving on the same Board.

-- Not have been removed from a school district office within the preceding year.

local.summary: Travelers at Buffalo-Niagara International Airport faced another day of delays and cancellations following a nationwide ground stop Friday that disrupted thousands of flights across the country.
local.body: Travelers at Buffalo-Niagara International Airport faced another day of delays and cancellations following a nationwide ground stop Friday that disrupted thousands of flights across the country.Among them was 5½-year-old Esakhan and his family, who were visiting relatives in Toronto and trying to return home to Atlanta.“Our flight got canceled yesterday and it was still canceled today,” Esakhan said.WATCH: 'Our flight got canceled': Travelers at Buffalo-Niagara International Airport facing cancellations, delaysHis mother said they were told their flight was delayed because of a shortage of flight attendants. “We're just hoping that our flight gets here soon and then we can leave,” she said.Across the country, more than 12,500 flights have been canceled since the FAA grounded virtually all flights for four hours Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on outdated technology that became overloaded.Flights have since resumed at Buffalo-Niagara International Airport, but many passengers were still dealing with the ripple effects.Kyle Johansen of Lockport said he and his wife were supposed to fly through Atlanta to Fort Lauderdale.“Now our Fort Lauderdale flight has been canceled and we're going to miss our cruise ship,” Johansen said.Another traveler headed back home New Orleans said he spent the night at the airport after his plans were disrupted, sleeping on a couch in the terminal.Other travelers faced hours-long delays. One couple said they were originally supposed to arrive in Phoenix at 6:30 p.m. but were now expecting to get there around 11:30 p.m.Another couple said they were told there was roughly a 50-50 chance their flight would leave after an additional three-hour delay. If not, they planned to go home and try again.For Johansen and his wife, there was eventually some good news.“We were able to get a connecting flight, hopefully,” Johansen said. “Hopefully we don't get stuck in Atlanta.”

entertainment.title: Lily Collins Pays Tribute to Phil Collins After Rock Hall Induction
entertainment.summary: Lily Collins said it felt “monumentally special” to watch her father Phil Collins inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame as a solo artist.
entertainment.body:
Lily Collins paid tribute to her father, Phil Collins , following his induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, saying it felt “monumentally special” to stand alongside her family as he accepted the honor. Explore Cynthia Erivo Genesis Lily Collins See latest videos, charts and news

The Emily in Paris star shared a series of photos from Saturday’s (Nov. 14) ceremony at Los Angeles’ Peacock Theater, where Collins was inducted as a solo artist — 16 years after he entered the Hall as a member of Genesis in 2010. Related Daniel Hall, Co-Founder of Australian Rock Band Taxiride, Dies at 48 U2 Opens 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Ceremony With Surprise Performance Phil Collins Tells Rock Hall Crowd: 'You Haven't Heard the Last of Me'

“To see my dad’s extraordinary legacy celebrated with an induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame is something I don’t think I’ll ever quite have the words for,” Lily wrote.

“Seeing you up there on stage embracing all the love, support, and recognition in the room after everything you’ve been through is indescribable,” she continued. “There is no one more deserving. We couldn’t be more proud. I couldn’t be more proud.”

Collins made a rare public appearance at the ceremony, where he was inducted by Travis Barker . He did not perform; Cynthia Erivo sang “In the Air Tonight” in his place, with Barker on drums.

Opening his acceptance speech, Collins told the crowd he’s “really not as bad as it looks,” before making a promise: “You haven’t heard the last of me. I promise you that.”

He went on to thank longtime manager Tony Smith, Atlantic Records’ Ahmet and Nesuhi Ertegun and Virgin Records founder Richard Branson, as well as “my three ex-wives, because they’ve loved me through the years and given me five great children.” He also credited his assistant with saving his life. “I’m not joking when I say without her I wouldn’t be here,” he said, adding that he’s “a well man now.”

The singer and drummer has faced significant health issues in recent years. A 2007 spinal injury caused nerve damage that left him unable to grip a drumstick, and he has since undergone knee surgeries and dealt with ongoing mobility problems. His son Nic played drums on Genesis ’ 2021-22 farewell tour, which wrapped in London in 2022, with Collins singing from a seated position.

entertainment.title: Johnny Depp fled Hollywood spotlight for quiet Bahamas life where ‘nobody’s pointing a camera at me’
entertainment.summary: During an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Depp opened up about craving privacy and not being able to have it in the United States.
entertainment.body:
Johnny Depp turns to the Bahamas to experience a private life.

During an interview with the Wall Street Journal , Depp opened up about craving privacy and not being able to have it in the United States.

“Today, I live most of the time in the Bahamas. It’s where I’ve found total peace and quiet. Nobody’s pointing a camera at me or staring. I bought my 1940s wood house in 2004 and added a yurt and a painting studio. Art continues to be a sanctuary that lets me process the world around me,” Depp told the outlet.

Depp famously purchased his own island in the Bahamas in 2004. In 2009, he told Vanity Fair that “escapism is survival to me,” and that, after playing a difficult role, “my head was done in. I needed to escape. So being able to get on the boat and move allowed my head freedom again.”

He continued, “Somehow, the mathematics led me here to my island. I don’t think I’d ever seen any place so pure and beautiful. You can feel your pulse rate drop about 20 beats. It’s instant freedom. And that rare beast—simplicity—can be had. And a little morsel of anonymity.”

The actor added, “Whenever I was getting frustrated about being ‘novelty boy’ and making movies, I told myself, Calm down. I can come down here and disappear.”

Depp told SCMP Style in 2023, “Where I feel the most myself in this world, and where I go to feel absolutely normal, I suppose, is my place in the Bahamas, because it’s an island and nobody’s looking at me.

“You’ve got to have some sanctuary, a safe place where you can escape the scrutiny and the interest of others, a place where you can just sit on a beach, read, paint, meditate or whatever, that’s freedom to me. That’s the only real freedom.”

entertainment.title: Dystopian Thriller ‘The Flaw’ Is a Cinematic Puzzle About Totalitarianism: “Each One of Us Is a Regime”
entertainment.summary: David Dawson is an interrogator of The Regime, and Arthur McBain is a suspect in a cat-and-mouse game in Theophilos Papastylianos' Tallinn-premiering debut feature, based on a bestselling novel.
entertainment.body:
In a dark, dystopian future, the Regime decides who belongs and who doesn’t. And the Regime puts the cold and calculating Interrogator on a man who becomes the Suspect to prove his guilt. He puts a ruthless plan of psychological manipulation into action. But could there be a shortcoming in the master plan?

The dystopian thriller The Flaw , a Greece–Latvia co-production, is based on Antonis Samarakis’ novel of the same name, which is a modern Greek classic and bestseller. It is also writer-director Theophilos Papastylianos’ ( Algorhythm , Showtime ) feature debut, and it is about to get its world premiere, appropriately in the Baltics. The film will debut in the Baltic Film Competition of the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) on Wednesday, Nov. 18. Related Stories Movies A Man Has Just Retired, But the Government Insists He Is Dead. Welcome to 'When I Existed'! (Exclusive Trailer, Plus Chat With the Directors) Lifestyle Soho House Creator Nick Jones Is Reinventing the Hotel -- Again

British talent leads The Flaw , with David Dawson, who plays Derek Jarman in Elsinore , portraying the Interrogator, and Arthur McBain ( After the Flood , Napoleon ) playing the Suspect. Also part of the ensemble cast are Ralf Little, Angela Brouskou, Lyne Renée, Sarah Akokhia and Georgia Small. Thodoris Zacharakis is the cinematographer, while Yannis Chalkiadakis is the editor. Produced by Panos Papahadzis and Papastylianos, the co-producers are Alise Rogule and Lina Yannopoulou. Jacques Kruger is the sales agent.

Papastylianos talked to THR ahead of the film’s premiere about just how timely and urgent The Flaw feels, its cast and visuals, and why the film is like one giant puzzle.

How did you approach adapting the novel after you read it? It was my second time reading the book, and it was a revelation for me because the perspective was completely different. I wasn’t reading it as a teenager, like the first time. Now, I was reading it as a director.

The most important part when I wrote the script was to take a step back and say, “Okay, this is an amazing idea, but the film is going to be released in five to seven years. Is it going to be amazing in seven years?”

It was instinct because I was seeing how the whole world was progressing and how society was changing. I felt this book was timeless, and as the years go by, it’s going to become more up to date all the time.

entertainment.title: ‘Kindergarten Cop’ villain breaks silence on death of on-screen son Christian Cousins
entertainment.summary: "Kindergarten Cop" star Richard Tyson paid tribute to former child actor Christian Cousins, who died at age 43 in Irvine, California.
entertainment.body:
“Kindergarten Cop” villain Richard Tyson has spoken out after the death of former child co-star Christian Cousins .

“I was saddened to hear of the passing of Christian Cousins, who, alongside his twin brother Joseph, starred with me in ‘Kindergarten Cop,’” Tyson wrote in a heartfelt Facebook tribute Sunday.

“It’s hard to believe that more than 35 years have passed since we made that film together.”

Tyson, who played the ruthless drug dealer Cullen Crisp — the on-screen father of Cousins’ character — in the 1990 action comedy, said Cousins was part of a remarkable cast that helped make “Kindergarten Cop” a movie that “continues to bring joy to audiences around the world.”

“My heartfelt condolences go out to his brother Joseph, his family, friends & all those who knew and loved him,” Tyson wrote.

“Rest in peace, Christian. You will always be part of our Kindergarten Cop family.”

Cousins, 43, was found dead at his home in Irvine, California, after concerned family members were unable to reach him.

Irvine police responded to a welfare check at his home just after noon on Oct. 20, TMZ reported.
